rashi:a1.1: And he answers: in order to publicize it — for the mother, that she is exempt from the firstborn [obligation]; for since we bury her clot, we treat it as presumptively an offspring.
rashi:a2.1: And he challenges: since you exempt her from the firstborn [obligation], that is to say it is a full-fledged offspring; then why does it not impart impurity?
rashi:a2.2: Nullification in a majority: that is why it does not impart impurity, because the flesh is nullified in the majority of blood and of membranes that come out with it.
rashi:a2.3: They touched upon it: what we said, that it does not impart impurity through contact, is because of nullification in a majority.
rashi:a4.1: The afterbirth in the house: the woman miscarried an afterbirth, and no offspring is recognizable in it.
rashi:a4.2: The house is impure: as it teaches the reason: there is no afterbirth without an offspring, only that it disintegrated; and even so it imparts impurity.
rashi:a4.3: Rabbi Shimon says: the offspring disintegrated: and we establish there that the reason of Rabbi Shimon, who says the house is pure, is because “they touched upon it due to nullification in a majority”, in Tractate Niddah, chapter HaMapelet (Niddah 27a).
rashi:a5.1: Opening of the grave: a woman whose fetus died in her womb, who sat on the birthstool, and the “grave” of the womb opened in this house, but the offspring did not come out, and they took her to another house: the first house is impure as if it had been born there, since impurity breaks through [and rises]. And likewise [the rule is that] there is no opening of the grave for miscarried fetuses, except for a miscarried fetus that has already rounded its head, that is, whose head has become thick.
rashi:a5.2: A skein of wool: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss.)
rashi:a5.3: Rabbi [my teacher], explain: whether a skein of warp, which is small, is required, or a skein of woof, which is large.
rashi:a6.1: He said to him: it is taught: that they disagree about it.
rashi:a6.2: From when tefifiyot are seen: Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Tzadok disagrees with the first tanna and says: even if they have not rounded the head like a skein, there is opening of the grave once her womb has opened so far that tefifiyot are seen inside her womb.
rashi:a6.3: Like a mule that bends down to pass water: it bends down more than a domesticated or wild animal, and through the bending its womb opens wide and folds appear in the womb.
rashi:a6.4: A skein within a skein: and this is tefifiyot — “pipi” twice over, and “pipi” is pika [a skein].
rashi:a7.1: And I do not have to explain: I do not know how to explain.
rashi:a7.2: Of a woman: [the measure] for the law that it has opening of the grave.
rashi:a7.3: Of an animal: [the measure] for it not to be like swallowed impurity, with regard to impurity through contact as the carcass of a miscarried fetus, if the shepherd stretched out his hand and touched it to bring it out of the womb.
rashi:a7.4: Like that of woof: once it has rounded its head like a skein of woof; and if not, it is swallowed impurity and does not impart impurity, as we learned: an animal whose fetus died inside its womb, and the shepherd stretched out his hand and touched it, he is pure — in chapter Behema HaMaksha (Ḥullin 70b).
rashi:a8.1: A clod: of earth; its measure to impart impurity in a tent, and to burn teruma and consecrated food on its account.
rashi:a8.2: Like a large skein of sack makers: martzufin are large sacks of reed, and when they close them they seal them.
rashi:a8.3: And it is found on the upper side of the stopper of a Bethlehem jug: that is, that seal [size] is found on the upper side of the cover made for earthenware jugs, which is broad at the bottom to cover the jug and narrows toward the top so it can be held by hand; that narrowing side he calls the upper side. Laḥmit: [jugs] made in Bethlehem [Beit Leḥem].
rashi:a9.1: Brings it into contact with water: [he needs to,] since perhaps it became impure through contact with the am ha’aretz.
rashi:a9.2: And it is pure: whichever way you look at it, for certainly water is mixed into it. If the water is the majority, the brine is nullified in the majority and it receives impurity on account of the water, and water can be purified through hashaka: he puts the vessel into the ritual bath until the water of the bath passes over its mouth and touches the water inside the vessel. And although food and liquids have no purification in a ritual bath, water is purified through hashaka, for it is like one who sowed them and took them up again, and sowing purifies from impurity, as we learned (Terumot 9:7): teruma seedlings that became impure and he replanted them are pure. I found this in a responsum of Rabbeinu Gershon [i.e., Rabbeinu Gershom].
rashi:a10.1: Brine is not susceptible to impurity: for it is merely sweat that comes out of the fish when they are salted.
rashi:a10.2: Because of that minority of water: which is susceptible to impurity, and hashaka does not help it, since the majority is brine and hashaka does not work for food; [nevertheless] it is nullified in the majority, and the brine is not impure.
rashi:a11.1: They taught only: that it is nullified in the majority and the brine is permitted, only for dipping his bread.
rashi:a11.2: But: to prepare a pot with it is forbidden, for the water in the brine finds the water in the pot, and they join together and become more than the brine, and render it impure.
rashi:a11.3: A type found its type and is revived: [it is revived] from the status of nullification and returns to impurity.
tosafot:a3.1: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon said the same thing: Although the Rabbis agree with Rabbi Shimon that it is nullified when they took it out in a bowl to the outer house, as is said in Niddah, chapter HaMapelet (Niddah 27a), nevertheless one can say “they said the same thing” only of Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov and Rabbi Shimon, since for both of them it is nullified at the start of the birth. And although the words of Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov do not imply nullification at all, and it is Rabbi Ḥiyya who says so, one can say that “Rabbi Ḥiyya teaches” means that he taught, within the words of Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov, that it imparts no impurity through contact or carrying; and so it appears explicitly in the Tosefta.
tosafot:a5.1: Until they round the head like a skein: What we learned in chapter HaMaksha (Ḥullin 70b), that an animal whose fetus died in its womb, and the shepherd stretched out his hand [and touched it], he is pure, is when it has not rounded [its head] like a skein. And likewise the other [mishna] taught there, a woman whose offspring died in her womb and the midwife stretched out [her hand and touched it], etc., the woman is pure until the offspring comes out; and the Gemara implies that she is pure because it is swallowed impurity, while the midwife is impure lest the offspring put its head out beyond the corridor without her noticing — this too speaks of when it has not rounded its head like a skein. One cannot say that it is always [rounded] like a skein and [the case is] before the opening of the grave, since [the midwife] is impure only by a decree lest it put its head out beyond the corridor, implying that before that she would be pure, even though the opening of the grave comes before that; for when the head comes out beyond the corridor it is like fully born.
tosafot:a8.1: On the upper side of the stopper of the jug: that stopper has a kind of handle made for holding it, and it is round like the thing called (Tosafot add an Old French gloss).
tosafot:a10.1: Those minorities of water are nullified in the majority: and it is not like other prohibitions, which [forbid] when they impart flavor, for [the principle that] flavor is like the substance itself was not said with regard to impurity. Likewise, a carcass is nullified in slaughtered meat with regard to impurity, even if everything was then cooked together.
tosafot:a10.2: They are nullified in the majority: and even if they were half and half, in any case, since [the water] is then not nullified, hashaka works for it.
tosafot:a11.1: But for a pot, no: a type found its type and is revived: This is not like what we say in chapter Gid HaNasheh (Ḥullin 100b), chapter HaKometz Rabba (Menaḥot 23a) and the last chapter of Avoda Zara (73a): remove its own type as if it were not there, and the other type exceeds it and nullifies it. For there its own type becomes forbidden only by force of the prohibited substance that was mixed into it and cannot be separated, and wherever it is, it is permitted; therefore it is apt to say “remove it.” But where its own type itself becomes impure through contact with the impure water, it is not apt to say “remove it.”
tosafot:a11.2: And is revived: The Kuntres [Rashi] explained that the water again becomes more than the brine and renders it impure. But he was not precise, for brine is not susceptible to impurity. Rather, this is the reviving: before this, the brine nullified the water from impurity as a liquid through the majority of brine, and now the water is revived to what it was at first, before it was mixed with the brine.
tosafot:a11.3: In brief: Rabbeinu Efrayim asks: here Rav Dimi holds that even purity revives impurity, yet in Avoda Zara 73a he holds that even a prohibition does not revive a prohibition, saying that when one pours libation wine from a barrel into a cistern, even all day long, each drop is nullified as it falls. Answer: here he speaks in the name of Reish Lakish, there in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan. But Rabbi Yoḥanan remains difficult: if even the impurity of non-sacred food, which is lenient, revives (as derived shortly from the mishna and baraita, “lest he bring a kav of impure non-sacred produce”), all the more so a prohibition should revive a prohibition, and that is plain throughout the Talmud (Yevamot 82b, “he put in a se’a and took out a se’a” is fit only up to the majority; Shabbat 142a, though that is a weaker proof); and in Nedarim 57b Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that even permitted growth raises the prohibited. Rabbeinu Tam distinguishes between additions without a break and with a break (Niddah 71b on the blood of tevusa; Zevaḥim 78a; Bava Kamma 100a; Bava Batra 2a), placing Avoda Zara’s case where the pouring stopped; but our passage and Yevamot speak of reviving even without a break. Tosafot’s teacher holds that reviving applies everywhere, even with a break: the blood of tevusa is a rabbinic leniency, mixed sacrificial blood is different because each drop is rejected as it falls, and Rabbi Yoḥanan’s “each drop is nullified” holds only while the permitted wine is sixty times the prohibited. Tosafot then discuss at length whether libation wine is nullified up to the majority or only up to sixty; prohibited falling into permitted versus permitted into prohibited; a thick stream of pouring; fruit juices; Rabbeinu Tam’s rulings on gentile wine that is permitted for benefit (not forbidden in any amount) and that the halakha follows Ravin (cf. Yevamot 64b), and whether Ravin disputes Rav Dimi and Rav Yitzḥak; Rav Shmuel son of Rabbi Yehuda’s requirement that a jug of water fall in first; and Rabbi Yoḥanan’s “diluted them and mixed them” (Pesaḥim). They conclude that these nullifications apply where one did not intend to nullify the prohibition or purify the impure, and that the amora of our brine passage does not hold “remove its own type as if it were not there.” Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:a1.1: And since it is exempt from the firstborn [obligation], we presume [the clot] to be an offspring; then why does it not impart impurity?
gershom:a2.1: They touched upon it due to nullification in a majority: it certainly has the form of an offspring; so why does it not impart impurity? Because it is nullified in the majority, in the blood.
gershom:a3.1: The afterbirth in the house: she miscarried only an afterbirth, in the house.
gershom:a4.1: The offspring disintegrated before it emerged: for it is nullified in the majority of blood, membranes and water in the afterbirth, and the house is pure.
gershom:a5.1: There is no opening of the grave for miscarried fetuses: [A printed note suggests the text should read: “Since the grave opened and the offspring had already completed its months,” etc.] An offspring that completed its months and died in its mother’s womb, for example when the woman sits on the birthstool — that is the opening of the grave: once the grave opens, when it overshadows the house with an opening of a handbreadth, from that moment the house is impure, even though it is not fully born until the next day. But miscarried fetuses that did not complete their months have no opening of the grave to render the house impure until the head is round like a skein, that is, until its form and the features of its face are complete and its head is as large as skeins of wool. And some explain “like a pika” as like the stone on which women begin to wind the threads.
gershom:a6.1: Of warp is small, and of woof is large.
gershom:a7.1: A skein within a skein: a round within a round, as seen in a female.
gershom:a8.1: A large skein: a large ball [of thread].
gershom:a9.1: Of sack makers: the threads of sackcloth, which are thick.
gershom:a10.1: A clod that comes: from the ground of a beit haperas.
gershom:a11.1: And from the land of the nations: it is like a beit haperas; since its measure is like a large skein, [we are concerned] lest there be in that earth a bone the size of a barley grain.
gershom:a12.1: And it is found: that measure.
gershom:a13.1: On the upper side of the stopper of a jug: the narrow part at the top is like a large skein.
gershom:a14.1: Laḥmit: which they make in Bethlehem [Beit Leḥem]; it is a place.
gershom:a15.1: Since he performed hashaka on it, it is pure from what became impure at the hands of the am ha’aretz.
gershom:a16.1: Brine is not susceptible to impurity: it is merely sweat.
gershom:a17.1: What is there: to be concerned about?
gershom:a18.1: If [it is] because of those minorities of water in it, which need hashaka, and it does not help them because they are a minority, so that the water would make the brine [impure] and bring impurity to it — one cannot say so, for this water is nullified in the majority and cannot bring impurity to it.
gershom:a19.1: They taught only: that they are nullified in the majority, only if he wants to dip his bread in that brine.
gershom:a20.1: But for a pot: if he wants to put the brine into a pot, the minority of water is not nullified relative to the brine.
gershom:a21.1: For a type found its type and is revived: that is, the minority of water in the brine renders the water in the pot impure, and they joined and became a majority, and it is revived from the status of nullification. This “revived” [ni’or] means something like “removed” [from nullification].
gershom:a22.1: And was saying this teaching: “They taught this only for dipping,” etc.
gershom:a23.1: But does impurity that was previously nullified in a majority return and revive? That is, that they combine to impart impurity.
rashi:b1.1: Into one hundred pure non-sacred: which had not been rendered susceptible [to impurity], and [the teruma] did not render them impure by falling in.
rashi:b1.2: Let it be lifted: let one lift a se’a from there and let it rot, according to the law of impure teruma, for I say, etc.; and impure teruma is forbidden to eat.
rashi:b2.1: Let it arise: let it be nullified and be eaten with its non-sacred produce; and because of a decree, he gives its value to the priests, or lifts a se’a from it to be eaten by priests.
rashi:b2.2: Nikkudim: dry, as in “it was dry and crumbled [nikkudim]” (Joshua 9:5). For now, even though there is impure and pure in it, the impure does not render the pure impure without its being rendered susceptible, and the impure is nullified in the pure, and it may be eaten dry.
rashi:b2.3: And roasted: likewise, for they are not rendered susceptible and do not receive impurity.
rashi:b2.4: Or kneaded with fruit juice: such as apple juice and mulberry juice, for fruit juices do not render [food] susceptible.
rashi:b3.1: Those non-sacred items according to Rabbi Eliezer, what will be with them: for according to the Rabbis we have already said, of all of them, both the non-sacred and the teruma, that it is to be eaten dry or roasted.
tosafot:b1.1: Let it be lifted and let it rot: In the Jerusalem Talmud it teaches “let it be burned.” And this is difficult: are we dealing with fools, who are permitted to benefit from burning it and do not wish to, and leave it to rot? There is no need to teach what people do not usually do. Rabbeinu Tam explains that “let it rot” and “let it be burned” are all one: our Gemara explains the mishna’s “let it be burned” as without benefit, like rotting, for if you permitted it for benefit he would come to eat it, since there was reason to permit it through nullification, as the Rabbis say, “let it arise and be eaten”; and this is what it means: either let it rot or let it be burned without benefit. One can also explain that it is a dispute between the Babylonians and the people of the Land of Israel, between our Talmud and the Jerusalem Talmud. Likewise, in another clause taught in that chapter, where it teaches, after they agreed, “Rabbi Eliezer says: let it be lifted and burned,” the Tosefta teaches “let it be lifted and rot”; it may be that some taught it this way and some that way. Likewise we find in chapter Mitzvat Ḥalitza (Yevamot 104b), regarding a minor girl who performed ḥalitza, that in our books we read “her ḥalitza is invalid” and in the Jerusalem Talmud they read “valid”; and at the start of Makom Shenahagu (Pesaḥim 51b), regarding “all aftergrowths are forbidden except aftergrowths of cabbage,” the reading is not so in the Jerusalem Talmud and the Mishnayot. And if you say: since it rots and is forbidden for benefit, why lift it out? The Jerusalem Talmud explains that orla and diverse kinds of the vineyard are nullified in two hundred and one and need not be lifted out, while teruma [is nullified] in one hundred and one and must be lifted out because of robbery of the tribe [of priests]; but here, since once it is lifted out it is forbidden, there is no robbery of the tribe. One can say that the Rabbis did not distinguish.
tosafot:b2.1: Let it arise and be eaten: The Kuntres [Rashi] explained: “let it arise” is an expression of nullification, not of lifting out, as it teaches “let it be lifted” according to Rabbi Eliezer and “let it arise” according to the Rabbis. And what we learned in the last chapter of Tractate Orla, that teruma and teruma of the tithe “arise” in one hundred and one and must be lifted out, there it is because of the priest’s loss, and if he gives him its value that is fine. And know this, for the latter clause teaches that orla and diverse kinds of the vineyard need not be lifted out, and even so the expression of “arising” is taught of them, as it teaches: one who had bundles of fenugreek of diverse kinds of the vineyard, etc., and it teaches “let them arise in two hundred and one.” Until here the words of the Kuntres. And he is right that he explained the reason as because of loss, as the Jerusalem Talmud also explains the reason as robbery of the tribe. However, although the main enactment is for this reason, it would seem reasonable that he cannot exempt himself with money, for Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis disagree in chapter Notel (Shabbat 142a) and in the first chapter of Temura (12a) only about medumma [a mixture containing teruma]: according to Rabbi Eliezer it renders the mixture medumma as certain teruma, and according to the Rabbis in proportion; but it is obvious that it has the sanctity of teruma.
tosafot:b2.2: Provided that there is not an egg-bulk in one place: meaning an egg-bulk of the teruma, for the teruma is one part in a hundred and one; [an egg-bulk of it] must not be [in one batch], for then there would be in it an egg-bulk of the impure teruma, and the impure cannot be nullified in a hundred of pure that has been rendered susceptible, for it renders everything impure, and it is like rendering teruma impure by hand, since the impure teruma became pure through its nullification. Yet for this reason alone it would not be forbidden: since the teruma was already nullified and everything is non-sacred and permitted to non-priests, what concern is there if one renders non-sacred food impure? Rather, it is required so that one does not mistakenly nullify a kav of impure non-sacred produce in a kav and a bit more, as [Ulla] explains on it, “what is the reason,” and [his explanation] applies both to Rabbi Eliezer and to the Rabbis. And if you say: when impure non-sacred produce is nullified in a majority of pure non-sacred produce, let us be concerned for this too — one can say that there, where a minority of impure non-sacred produce is nullified in a majority of pure, there is no concern lest he bring a kav of impure non-sacred produce and a kav and a bit more of this kind, since it is known that the name of impurity did not leave the impure non-sacred produce mixed into the pure. But here he thinks the name of impurity left it entirely, since we permit everything to be eaten by non-priests according to the Rabbis, or the non-sacred produce according to Rabbi Eliezer, even though the teruma is mixed in with it.
gershom:b1.1: Let it be lifted and let it rot: let one take a se’a from it, and let it rot according to the law of impure teruma, which has no remedy.
gershom:b2.1: That is why it rots: for I say, etc.
gershom:b3.1: And the Rabbis say: let it arise: that is, he separates a se’a from it.
gershom:b4.1: And be eaten: that se’a itself.
gershom:b5.1: Nikkudim: that is, dry, parched and wiped, without anything that renders it susceptible.
gershom:b6.1: Or roasted, or kneaded with fruit juice: which do not receive impurity.
gershom:b7.1: Or divided into doughs: so that there is not an egg-bulk of them in one place, and the rest is fully non-sacred.
